alignment.note: Greek expresses the indefinite locative with ὅπου ἐάν (two words, conjunction plus conditional particle); the Peshitta fuses the relative-locative into the single prefixed form ܘܠܐܝܟܐ, and the Vulgate compresses both into the single relative adverb quocumque. The notional value is identical but the morphosyntactic packaging differs across all three.

Greek εἰσέλθῃ is aorist subjunctive ('he may enter'), suiting the indefinite ὅπου ἐάν construction, whereas the Peshitta ܕܥܐܠ employs a participle/imperfect-style relative ('where he enters'); the Vulgate introierit is future-perfect, all three rendering the open conditional differently in tense-aspect.

Greek uses the single compound noun οἰκοδεσπότῃ ('householder'); both the Peshitta (ܠܡܪܐ ܒܝܬܐ, 'to the lord of the house') and the Vulgate (domino domus, 'to the master of the house') unpack the compound into a construct/genitive phrase, a routine analytic rendering of the Greek lexeme.

Greek ὅτι recitativum introduces direct speech and is matched by Latin quia; the Peshitta omits any complementiser, simply juxtaposing the quoted clause, which is the normal Syriac means of introducing reported speech.

Greek ὁ διδάσκαλος ('the Teacher') and Latin magister both render the title transparently, while the Peshitta uses ܪܒܢ ('our master/Rabban'), a culturally embedded honorific that adds a first-person-plural possessive nuance absent from the Greek and Latin.
λέγει / ܐܡܪ / dicit (Vulgate adds the colon as quotation punctuation).

Greek ποῦ ἐστιν and Latin Ubi est both use two words (interrogative adverb plus copula); the Peshitta contracts this into the single enclitic form ܐܝܟܘ ('where-is-it'), a standard Syriac univerbation of the interrogative with the pronominal copula.

Greek τὸ κατάλυμά μου ('my guest-room') is matched by Latin refectio mea, but the Peshitta renders ܒܝܬ ܡܫܪܝܐ ('house of lodging'), a construct expression for a guest-lodging that lacks the explicit possessive suffix present in both the Greek and Latin.

The Greek and Latin both place the object πάσχα / Pascha before the prepositional phrase and the verb at the end (τὸ πάσχα μετὰ τῶν μαθητῶν μου φάγω / Pascha cum discipulis meis manducem), whereas the Syriac inverts the order, placing the verb ܕܐܟܘܠ first and the object ܦܨܚܐ last (ܐܟܘܠ ... ܦܨܚܐ); this is a word-order divergence with no semantic change, and the Peshitta omits an explicit equivalent of the article τό.

The Vulgate marks the interrogative force with a closing question mark, a punctuational feature corresponding to the Greek question particle in φάγω; (semicolon = Greek question mark); the Peshitta has no terminal punctuation token.
